title: Part 6, Chapter 3
paragraphs: He hurried to Svidrigailov. What he hoped to get from the man, he didn't know. But Svidrigailov held some hidden power over him. Having once recognized this, he couldn't rest — and now the time had come.
On the way, one question nagged at him in particular: had Svidrigailov been to see Porfiry?
As far as he could tell, he would have sworn he hadn't. He went over it again and again, reviewed Porfiry's visit in his mind — no, he definitely hadn't gone. Of course not.

But if he hadn't gone yet, would he? For the moment, Raskolnikov felt he wouldn't. Why? He couldn't have explained, and even if he could, he wouldn't have wasted much thought on it just then. It all worried him, yet at the same time he couldn't focus on it. Strangely — no one would have believed it perhaps — he felt only a faint, vague anxiety about his immediate future. A different, far more important concern tormented him: it was about himself, but in a different, more fundamental way. On top of it all, he was conscious of immense moral exhaustion, though his mind was working better that morning than it had recently.

And was it even worth it, after everything that had happened, to keep struggling over these petty details? Was it worth maneuvering to keep Svidrigailov from going to Porfiry? Was it worth investigating, wasting time on someone like Svidrigailov?
Oh, how sick he was of it all!

And yet he was hurrying to Svidrigailov — could he be expecting something new from him? Information? A way out? People will clutch at straws! Was it fate, or some instinct drawing them together? Perhaps it was just exhaustion, despair. Perhaps it wasn't Svidrigailov he needed at all, but someone else, and Svidrigailov had simply presented himself. Sonia? But why would he go to Sonia now? To beg for her tears again? He was afraid of Sonia too. Sonia represented an irrevocable sentence. He had to go his own way or hers. Right now especially, he didn't feel equal to facing her. No — wouldn't it be better to try Svidrigailov? And he couldn't help acknowledging inwardly that for some reason he'd long felt he had to see him.

But what could they possibly have in common? Even their wickedness couldn't be the same kind. The man was deeply unpleasant — clearly depraved, undoubtedly cunning and deceitful, possibly malicious. Such stories circulated about him. True, he was helping Katerina Ivanovna's children, but who knew his motives? The man always had some scheme, some hidden agenda.

There was another thought that had been circling Raskolnikov's mind recently, causing him great distress. It was so painful he made deliberate efforts to push it away. He sometimes thought Svidrigailov was tracking him. Svidrigailov had discovered his secret and had designs on Dunya. What if he still did? Wasn't it practically certain? And what if, having discovered his secret and gained power over him, Svidrigailov intended to use it as a weapon against Dunya?

This idea sometimes tormented even his dreams, but it had never presented itself so vividly as now, on his way to Svidrigailov. The very thought filled him with dark rage. To begin with, it would change everything — even his own situation. He might have to confess his secret to Dunya immediately. Would he have to turn himself in, perhaps, to prevent Dunya from doing something rash? The letter? That morning Dunya had received a letter. Who in Petersburg would be writing to her? Luzhin, maybe? True, Razumikhin was there to protect her, but Razumikhin knew nothing about the situation. Maybe it was his duty to tell Razumikhin? He thought of it with revulsion.

In any case, he had to see Svidrigailov as soon as possible — that much was clear. Thank God, the specifics of their conversation didn't matter much, if only he could get to the heart of the matter. But if Svidrigailov were plotting against Dunya...
Raskolnikov was so drained by everything he'd been through that month that he could only resolve such questions one way: "Then I'll kill him," he thought in cold despair.

A sudden anguish gripped his heart. He stopped in the middle of the street and looked around, trying to get his bearings. He found himself on X— Prospect, thirty or forty paces from the Hay Market, which he'd just come through. The entire second floor of the building to his left was a tavern. All the windows were open; judging by the figures moving behind them, the rooms were packed. Sounds of singing poured out — clarinet, violin, and the boom of a Turkish drum. He could hear women shrieking. He was about to turn back, wondering why he'd come this way, when suddenly, in one of the far windows, he spotted Svidrigailov. He was sitting at a tea table right by the open window, pipe in mouth. Raskolnikov was taken aback, almost terrified. Svidrigailov was watching him silently, studying him — and, what struck Raskolnikov at once, seemed to be on the verge of getting up and slipping away unnoticed. Raskolnikov immediately pretended not to have seen him, gazing absently in another direction while watching him from the corner of his eye. His heart was pounding. And yes — Svidrigailov clearly didn't want to be seen. He took the pipe from his mouth and was about to duck out of sight, but as he stood and pushed back his chair, he apparently realized Raskolnikov had spotted him. What passed between them was much like their first meeting in Raskolnikov's room. A sly smile appeared on Svidrigailov's face, growing wider and wider. Each knew the other had seen him. Finally Svidrigailov burst out laughing.
"Well, come in if you want me — I'm here!" he shouted from the window.

Raskolnikov went up to the tavern. He found Svidrigailov in a tiny back room adjoining the main hall, where merchants, clerks, and all sorts of people were drinking tea to the frantic bellowing of a chorus. The click of billiard balls could be heard in the distance. On the table before Svidrigailov stood an open bottle and a glass half full of champagne. Also in the room were a boy with a small hand organ and a healthy-looking, rosy-cheeked girl of about eighteen in a tucked-up striped skirt and a Tyrolean hat with ribbons. Despite the chorus in the other room, she was singing some servants' hall ditty in a rather husky contralto, accompanied by the organ.

"That's enough," Svidrigailov stopped her as Raskolnikov entered. The girl immediately broke off and stood waiting respectfully. She had been singing her vulgar lyrics with a serious, almost reverential expression.
"Hey, Philip — a glass!" Svidrigailov called out.
"I won't have anything to drink," said Raskolnikov.
"Suit yourself — it wasn't for you anyway. Drink up, Katia! I don't need anything more today — you can go." He poured her a full glass and laid down a yellow banknote.

Katia drank her wine in one long series of gulps, the way women do, without setting down the glass, took the money, kissed Svidrigailov's hand — which he accepted with complete seriousness — and left. The boy trailed out after her with the organ. Both had been picked up from the street. Svidrigailov hadn't been in Petersburg a week, yet everything around him already had a patriarchal quality. The waiter Philip was by now an old friend, thoroughly obsequious.
The door to the main room had a lock on it. Svidrigailov was at home in this little room and probably spent whole days here. The tavern was dirty and wretched — not even second-rate.

"I was on my way to see you and looking for you," Raskolnikov began, "but I don't know what made me turn onto X— Prospect from the Hay Market just now. I never take this route. I usually turn right from the Hay Market. And this isn't the way to your place either. I just turned — and here you are. Strange!"
"Why not just say outright: 'It's a miracle'?"
"Because it might just be coincidence."

"Oh, that's how you people all think!" Svidrigailov laughed. "You won't admit it even when you secretly believe it's miraculous! You just said yourself it 'might' be only coincidence. And what cowards everyone is here about having their own opinion — you can't imagine, Rodion Romanovitch. I don't mean you — you have your own opinions and aren't afraid of them. That's what first attracted my interest."
"Nothing else?"
"Well, that's enough, isn't it?" Svidrigailov was obviously in high spirits, but only slightly so — he'd had no more than half a glass of wine.
"I think you came to see me before you knew I was capable of having what you call opinions of my own," Raskolnikov observed.

"Oh well, that was a different matter. Everyone has their own plans. And speaking of miracles — let me tell you, I think you've been sleeping for the last two or three days. I told you about this tavern myself; there's no miracle in your coming straight here. I described the route, gave you the address, and told you what hours you'd find me. Remember?"
"I don't remember," Raskolnikov answered with surprise.

"I believe you. I told you twice. The address got stamped on your memory mechanically. You turned this way mechanically, following the directions exactly, without being aware of it. When I told you, I hardly thought you'd understood. You give yourself away too easily, Rodion Romanovitch. And another thing: I'm convinced lots of people in Petersburg talk to themselves as they walk. It's a city of half-mad people. If only we had scientists — doctors, lawyers, and philosophers could conduct the most valuable research here, each in their own field. Few places exert so many gloomy, powerful, and strange influences on the human soul as Petersburg. The climate alone does so much. And it's the administrative center of all Russia — its character must radiate across the whole country. But that's neither here nor there. The point is: I've watched you several times. You leave your building holding your head high. Twenty paces from home, you let it drop and fold your hands behind your back. You look around but clearly see nothing in front of you or beside you. Eventually you start moving your lips, talking to yourself — sometimes waving a hand and declaiming — and then you just stop dead in the middle of the road. That's really not a good idea. Someone besides me might be watching, and it won't do you any good. It's really none of my business and I can't cure you, but you understand what I mean."
"Do you know that I'm being followed?" Raskolnikov asked, looking at him searchingly.
"No, I know nothing about that," Svidrigailov replied, seeming surprised.
"Well then, let's leave me out of it," Raskolnikov muttered with a frown.
"Fine, let's leave you out of it."

"Why don't you tell me this: if you come here to drink, and twice directed me to meet you here, why were you just trying to hide and get away when I looked up at the window from the street? I saw you."
"He-he! And why was it that you lay on your sofa with your eyes closed, pretending to be asleep, when you were wide awake the whole time I stood in your doorway? I saw that too."
"I may have had... my reasons. You know that yourself."
"And I may have had mine — though you don't know them."

Raskolnikov dropped his right elbow on the table, rested his chin on his right hand, and stared intently at Svidrigailov. For a full minute he studied that face, which had struck him before. It was a strange face, like a mask: white and ruddy, with bright red lips, a flaxen beard, and still-thick flaxen hair. His eyes were somehow too blue and their expression somehow too heavy and fixed. There was something deeply unsettling about that handsome face, which looked remarkably young for his age. Svidrigailov was smartly dressed in light summer clothes and particularly fastidious about his linen. He wore a massive ring with a precious stone.

"Do I really have to concern myself with you too?" Raskolnikov said suddenly, getting straight to the point with nervous impatience. "Even if you're perhaps the most dangerous man alive and decide to harm me, I'm not going to play games anymore. I'll show you right now that I don't value my own safety as highly as you probably think. I've come to tell you directly: if you persist in your former intentions toward my sister, and if you think you can profit from what's been recently discovered, I will kill you before you can have me locked up. You can count on that. You know I keep my word. And secondly, if there's something you want to tell me — because I keep getting the feeling you have something to say — then say it quickly. Time is short, and soon it may be too late."
"What's the rush?" Svidrigailov asked, studying him with curiosity.
"Everyone has their plans," Raskolnikov answered darkly and impatiently.

"You're the one who just demanded frankness, yet at the first question you refuse to answer," Svidrigailov observed with a smile. "You keep imagining I have hidden motives, so naturally you look at me with suspicion. That's perfectly understandable in your position. Much as I'd like us to be friends, I won't trouble myself trying to prove otherwise. It's not worth the effort, and I had nothing particularly special to discuss with you."
"Then what did you need me for? You're the one who kept hanging around."

"Simply as an interesting subject for study. I liked the fantastical nature of your situation — that's all! Besides, you're the brother of someone who interested me greatly, and I used to hear a great deal about you from that person. I gathered you had quite an influence over her — isn't that enough? Ha-ha-ha! Still, I must admit your question is rather complicated and hard for me to answer. Here, for instance — you came to me not just with a specific purpose but also hoping to hear something new, didn't you? Isn't that right?" Svidrigailov persisted with a sly smile. "Well, can't you imagine that I too, on the train coming here, was counting on you — on you telling me something new, on my getting some profit from you! You see what rich men we are!"
"What profit could you get?"

"How would I know? How could I? You see what kind of tavern I spend my time in — and I enjoy it, or rather, it's not much of an enjoyment, but you have to sit somewhere. That poor Katia just now — did you see her?... If only I were a gourmand, a club gourmet — but look what I eat!"
He pointed to a small table in the corner where the remains of a ghastly-looking beefsteak and potatoes sat on a tin plate.

"Have you eaten, by the way? I've had something and don't want any more. I don't drink at all, for instance — nothing except champagne, and not more than a glass all evening, and even that gives me a headache. I ordered this just now to wind myself up, because I'm heading out somewhere and you find me in a peculiar mood. That's why I tried to hide from you just now, like a schoolboy — I was afraid you'd get in my way. But I think" — he pulled out his watch — "I can spend an hour with you. It's half past four now. If only I were something — a landowner, a father, a cavalry officer, a photographer, a journalist... I'm nothing, no particular occupation, and sometimes I'm positively bored. I honestly thought you'd tell me something new."
"But who are you, really? And why have you come here?"
"Who am I? A gentleman. I served two years in the cavalry, then knocked around Petersburg for a while, then married Marfa Petrovna and lived in the country. There's my biography!"
"You're a gambler, I believe?"
"No — a poor excuse for one. A card-sharp, not a gambler."
"You've been a card-sharp?"
"Yes, I've been a card-sharp too."
"Did you ever get beaten for it?"
"It happened. Why?"
"Well, you could have challenged them to a duel... All in all, it must have been lively."
"I won't argue with you. And besides, I'm no philosopher. I confess I came here mainly for the women."
"Right after burying Marfa Petrovna?"
"Quite so," Svidrigailov smiled with disarming candor. "And? You seem to find something wrong in my talking about women that way."
"You're asking whether I find something wrong with depravity?"

"Depravity! So that's your angle! Well, I'll answer in order — first about women in general, since I do like to talk. Tell me, why should I restrain myself? Why give up women when I have a passion for them? It's an occupation, at least."
"So the only thing you're after here is depravity?"

"Very well — depravity then. You insist on calling it depravity. But at least I appreciate a direct question. In this depravity, at least there's something constant, something rooted in nature rather than dependent on fantasy — something present in the blood like an eternal flame, always burning, not easily extinguished even with the years. You'll agree that's a kind of occupation."
"That's nothing to celebrate. It's a disease — and a dangerous one."

"Oh, is that what you think? I agree it's a disease, like anything taken to excess. And of course, one must practice moderation. But first of all, everyone goes to excess one way or another; and secondly, naturally one should be moderate and sensible, however pathetic it may sound. But what else am I supposed to do? If I didn't have this, I might have to shoot myself. I'm willing to admit that a decent person should endure boredom, but still..."
"And could you actually shoot yourself?"

"Oh, come!" Svidrigailov deflected with disgust. "Please don't talk about that," he added hurriedly, without any of the swagger he'd shown throughout the conversation. His face completely changed. "I'll confess to a shameful weakness — I'm afraid of death, and I don't like hearing it discussed. Did you know I'm something of a mystic?"
"Ah — the apparitions of Marfa Petrovna! Are they still visiting you?"

"Oh, don't talk about them! There haven't been any more in Petersburg, thank God!" he cried irritably. "Let's talk about something else... though... Hmm! I haven't much time and can't stay long with you. Pity! I'd have plenty to tell you."
"What's your engagement — a woman?"
"Yes, a woman — something that came up by chance... No, that's not what I want to discuss."
"And the squalor, the filth of everything around you — doesn't it affect you? Have you lost the strength to stop?"

"You're claiming to have such strength yourself? Ha-ha-ha! You surprise me, Rodion Romanovitch — though I knew you'd say something like that. You preach to me about vice and aesthetics! You — a Schiller, an idealist! Of course, that's all as it should be, and it would be strange if it weren't — yet it does seem odd in practice... Ah, what a shame I have no time. You're a most fascinating character! By the way — are you fond of Schiller? I'm terribly fond of him."
"What a braggart you are," Raskolnikov said with some disgust.

"I swear I'm not!" Svidrigailov laughed. "But I won't argue — let me be a braggart. Why not brag if it hurts no one? I lived seven years in the country with Marfa Petrovna, so when I come across an intelligent person like you — intelligent and highly interesting — I'm simply glad of the conversation. Besides, I've drunk that half-glass of champagne and it's gone slightly to my head. And there's a certain matter that's wound me up considerably — but I'll keep quiet about that... Where are you going?" he asked in alarm.
Raskolnikov had begun to get up. He felt oppressed and stifled, somehow uneasy about having come. He was now convinced that Svidrigailov was the most worthless scoundrel on the face of the earth.

"Wait! Stay a little!" Svidrigailov begged. "At least let them bring you some tea. Sit down — I won't ramble on about myself, I promise. I'll tell you something. Would you like to hear how a woman once tried to 'save' me, as you'd put it? It would actually answer your first question, since the woman in question was your sister. May I? It'll help pass the time."
"Go ahead — but I trust you won't..."
"Oh, don't worry. Besides, even in a worthless, despicable man like me, Avdotya Romanovna can inspire nothing but the deepest respect."
